teaser: Dug up in 1896 with his eyes still in place, staring at the men who found him.
review_notes:
Discovery: French School excavations at Delphi, spring 1896, in two parts (lower body first, then upper), north of the Temple of Apollo; buried by the 373 BC earthquake/rockfall.
Dedication by Polyzalos of Gela for a Pythian victory in 478 or 474 BC; inscription on the base partly recut.
Eyes: white paste/glass with dark stone; copper lashes and lips; silver in the headband meander and reportedly on the teeth (not visible in this photo, so teeth are not mentioned).
Height about 1.80 m. The photo shows only the upper two thirds; the claim about a deliberately elongated lower body is the usual explanation and is given as such.
The reins in the hand are partly ancient and partly restored; text avoids claiming either.

lesson.text: Spring 1896, on a mountainside at Delphi. French archaeologists have moved an entire village to dig beneath it. One day a workman's pick meets green metal: a long pleated skirt and two bare feet. A few days later, some yards away, the upper half appears. When the earth is brushed from the face, the diggers find a pair of eyes looking back at them.

That was the shock. Greek bronzes almost never survive, and when they do, the eye sockets are empty holes. This young man came out of the ground with his gaze intact after more than 2,300 years in the dark. The men on the dig had read about statues like this. None of them had ever seen one.

lesson.title: A face with its inlays
lesson.text: Bronze was only the start. The face is assembled from several materials.

spots.title: The eyes
spots.text: White paste for the eyeball, a dark stone for the iris, set into the bronze. Tiny copper lashes still fringe the lids. The gaze is level and a little to his right.

spots.title: The lips
spots.text: The lips were made of a redder metal than the skin, copper against bronze. They are closed and barely parted. He is not shouting, not even smiling.

spots.title: The victor's band
spots.text: A ribbon is tied around his head, the mark of a winner. Its key pattern, a running line of right angles called a meander, was inlaid in silver.

lesson.text: So the dull green you see is not what Greeks saw. Fresh bronze is the color of a suntanned body, somewhere between gold and brown. Picture warm skin, red lips, white eyes, a silver band flashing in mountain light. The green is corrosion, the mark of centuries underground.

An earthquake saved him. In 373 BC rocks and earth came down the slope at Delphi and buried the monument. Anything left standing in the sanctuary was later carried off or melted for its metal. Being lost was the only way to last.

Who was he? A driver, and probably not a famous one. Chariot racing was the most expensive sport in Greece. The glory went to the owner of the horses, the way a trophy today goes to the stable. A stone base found nearby names the man who paid: Polyzalos, ruler of Gela, a Greek city in Sicily.

His team won at the Pythian Games, held at Delphi in honor of the god Apollo, in the 470s BC. To thank the god and advertise the win, he ordered a life-size bronze group: four horses, a chariot, perhaps a groom, and the driver. Of all that, only fragments and this figure remain.
The Charioteer is the surviving piece of a much larger monument, and it honors the owner who paid, not the young man who drove.
Follow his arms and you can rebuild the missing chariot in your head. One of them still does its job. The other tells you how violently the statue was torn from its setting.
He drove with both hands. One arm is gone. Tap the place where it broke away.

spots.title: The empty sleeve
spots.text: The left arm ended here, at the edge of the short sleeve. You can see into the hollow bronze: the statue is a shell a few millimeters thick, cast in separate parts and joined.

lesson.text: That hollow tells you how he was made. The method is lost-wax casting: a wax model over a clay core is wrapped in more clay, the wax is melted out, and molten bronze is poured into the gap. Head, arms, torso, skirt and feet were cast one by one, then fitted together.

His right hand is still closed around the reins, held low and loose. That matters. If the horses were at full gallop, his arms would be tense and his clothes flying. Everything is still. Most likely this is the moment after the race, the slow parade in front of the crowd.

His long tunic is real sportswear. It is called a xystis, and drivers wore it down to the ankles. Cords ran over the shoulders and under the arms to keep the cloth from filling with air like a sail at racing speed.

The sculptor uses that garment to build the figure. Above the belt the cloth is loose and alive. Below it, the folds drop straight and regular. Many people see a column in that skirt, and it gives the figure the calm of a building.

spots.title: Soft sideburns
spots.text: Fine curls creep down in front of the ear, lightly scratched into the cheek. It is the first beard of a very young man, perhaps still in his teens.

spots.title: The driving hand
spots.text: Fingers and thumb close gently on the flat straps. The grip is relaxed, the wrist steady. Veins and knuckles are modeled with real attention.

spots.title: The gathered sleeve
spots.text: Cloth bunches over the shoulder in tight ripples where the cord pulls it in. Each ridge was shaped in the wax before casting.

spots.title: The V of the neckline
spots.text: The folds fall from both shoulders and meet in a point at the chest, then hang with their own weight. Nothing is symmetrical to the millimeter.

spots.title: The belt
spots.text: Set high, well above the natural waist. It makes the skirt very long, which may have corrected his proportions for viewers looking up at him in the chariot.

spots.title: Column folds
spots.text: Deep parallel grooves, like the fluting cut into a Greek column. No two are quite the same width, so the cloth still looks like cloth.

lesson.text: Art historians place him at a turning point. The stiff smiling statues of the previous century are gone, and the twisting, emotional bodies of later Greek art have not arrived. This in-between moment, around 480 to 450 BC, is called the Severe style: serious faces, simple forms, quiet poses.
Greek artists of this generation chose to show self-control instead of triumph. The winner's glory lies in how calm he stays.

He has barely left home since. The statue is kept in the museum at Delphi, a short walk from the spot where it stood and fell. Most great Greek bronzes are known only from Roman marble copies. This one is the original.

Go back to the diggers of 1896, kneeling in the dirt in front of that face. What unsettled them still works on visitors today. He does not look at you. He looks past you, at something he is still holding steady.

quiz.question: What astonished the excavators in 1896?
options: The statue was made of gold
The inlaid eyes were still in place
quiz.explanation: Greek bronzes usually lose their eyes; his survived.

quiz.question: Who paid for the monument?
options: Polyzalos, ruler of Gela in Sicily
quiz.explanation: The base names Polyzalos, whose team won at the Pythian Games.

quiz.question: Why did the statue survive when most Greek bronzes were melted down?
options: It was too heavy to move
An earthquake in 373 BC buried it
quiz.explanation: Rocks and earth covered the monument before it could be reused.

quiz.question: What moment does the calm pose most likely show?
quiz.explanation: Still arms and hanging cloth suggest the slow lap after the race.

quiz.question: What is the Severe style?
options: Greek art of about 480 to 450 BC, with serious faces and simple forms
A Roman fashion for copying statues
quiz.explanation: It is the sober phase between stiff early statues and later, more emotional ones.

quiz.question: What were the cords over his shoulders for?
options: To stop the tunic from billowing at speed
quiz.explanation: They held the xystis close to the body during the race.

facts.text: The green color of the statue is what the ancient Greeks saw.
facts.explanation: New bronze looked like tanned skin; the green is corrosion from burial.

facts.text: The statue was cast in several pieces that were then joined.
facts.explanation: Head, arms, torso, skirt and feet were cast separately by the lost-wax method.

facts.text: The Charioteer originally stood alone on a column.
facts.explanation: He was part of a group with a chariot and four horses.
